provenance.pipeline: satsuki v1 (v1.0.1 editorial re-edit: usage-note reshaping corpus-wide, lane discrimination for same-surface families, against prompts/style.md)

patterns.usage_note: Defines a term: the term comes first and the rest of the sentence says what it means, usually closing with ことだ, ものだ or という意味だ (遅刻とは…間に合わないことだ). The other entry is surprise at an unexpected fact (合格するとは驚いた), following a plain-form clause and ending in an evaluation or in nothing. The term is usually a noun, and とは is written-style; というのは is the neutral equivalent and って the casual spoken one.

examples.ruby: 幸[しあわ]せとは、他人[たにん]と比[くら]べないことだと思[おも]う。
examples.english: Happiness, I think, means not measuring yourself against others.

examples.ruby: 遅刻[ちこく]とは、決[き]めた時間[じかん]に間[ま]に合[あ]わないことだ。
examples.english: Being late means not making it there by the time you agreed on.

examples.ruby: 敬語[けいご]とは相手[あいて]を立[た]てるための道具[どうぐ]です。
examples.english: Honorific language is a tool for showing deference to the person you're dealing with.

patterns.usage_note: Defines a word or category in speech: a bare noun sits in front and what follows says what it denotes, usually closing on ものだ, ことだ, or a plain paraphrase (おやつってのは、食事の間に食べる軽い物だ). The sibling lane instead raises a topic and comments on it, taking a whole clause and landing on an evaluation or complaint (毎朝早く起きるってのは大変だ). ってのは is the spoken contraction; in writing the same definition takes とは or というのは.

examples.ruby: 友達[ともだち]ってのは、困[こま]った時[とき]に分[わ]かるものだよ。
examples.english: You only find out who your real friends are when you're in trouble.

examples.ruby: おやつってのは、食事[しょくじ]の間[あいだ]に食[た]べる軽[かる]い物[もの]だよ。
examples.english: A snack, basically, is something light you eat between meals.

examples.ruby: 相棒[あいぼう]ってのは、背中[せなか]を預[あず]けられる相手[あいて]だ。
examples.english: A partner is someone you can trust to watch your back.
